readerTitle: Why Avis bragged about being No. 2
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Avis, Hertz, 1962년 DDB 광고 캠페인) + 가상 적용 (동네 두 번째 피자 가게)
insight: 1등이 이미 고객 머릿속을 차지하고 있다면, 1등과의 관계 속에서 자기 자리를 정하고 약점을 솔직히 인정하는 편이 강점을 믿게 만든다.
misconception: 포지셔닝은 무조건 '우리가 최고'라고 주장하는 것이고, 약점을 인정하면 손님이 떠난다.

sources.text: Avis 'We try harder' 광고 캠페인 (Doyle Dane Bernbach, 1962년 시작). 광고 원문은 광고사 아카이브와 다수의 광고사 문헌에서 확인 가능
Ries, A. & Trout, J. (1981). Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind. McGraw-Hill. Avis 사례와 이후 'No. 1' 캠페인 비판
Townsend, R. (1970). Up the Organization. Knopf. 1960년대 Avis 사장 시절 회고

factChecks.note: 캠페인 시작 연도(1962년)와 광고사(DDB), 카피라이터 Paula Green, 아트디렉터 Helmut Krone의 참여를 광고사 자료로 확인하세요.
캠페인 전 Avis가 '오랫동안 적자'였다는 점(흔히 13년으로 인용)과 약 1년 만에 흑자로 돌아섰다는 점은 널리 인용되지만 1차 재무 자료로 확인이 필요합니다. 카드에는 숫자 없이 'for years', 'reportedly'로만 적었습니다.
광고 시안이 소비자 조사에서 반응이 좋지 않았는데도 집행했다는 이야기는 일화에 가깝습니다. 카드에 'reportedly'로 표시했습니다.
이후 'Avis is going to be No. 1' 류의 캠페인과 그에 대한 비판은 Ries & Trout(1981)의 주장입니다. 카드에서도 그들의 평가로 표현했습니다. 정확한 문구와 시기를 원문으로 확인하세요.
직원들이 'We try harder' 배지를 달았다는 점, 슬로건이 수십 년간 쓰였다는 점을 Avis 회사 연혁 자료로 확인하세요. 시장점유율 수치는 자료마다 달라 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why Avis bragged about being No. 2
body: In 1962, a car rental company ran ads admitting it was not the biggest. Hertz was No. 1, and everyone knew it.
Advertising rules said you never point out your weakness. Avis put it in the headline.

image.label: A silver medal on a podium next to a gold one
image.brief: 1960년대 잡지 광고 느낌의 일러스트. 시상대 위 1등 자리는 그림자 속에 있고, 2등 자리에 놓인 자동차 열쇠가 조명을 받음. 실제 Avis·Hertz 로고, 빨간·노란 브랜드 색 조합은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You're No. 2, losing money, against a famous leader.
body: It's the early 1960s. Avis is the second-largest car rental company and has lost money for years. Hertz is far bigger and better known.
Your ad agency brings you three directions. Which do you run?

options.feedback: It sounds confident, but every rival says the same. Customers know Hertz is bigger, so the claim is easy to ignore.

options.text: "We're only No. 2. So we try harder."
options.feedback: It admits what customers already believe, then turns it into a reason to choose you. The risk: you must actually deliver the extra effort.

options.text: "Same cars, lower prices than the leader"
options.feedback: Price gets attention, but a bigger rival can match it. And you're already losing money.

cards.title: Avis ran the No. 2 ad.
body: The agency Doyle Dane Bernbach wrote: *Avis is only No. 2 in rent a cars. So why go with us? We try harder.* The ads promised cleaner cars, full gas tanks and shorter lines, because a No. 2 can't afford to be lazy.

The idea reportedly tested poorly before launch. Avis ran it anyway. The company is widely reported to have returned to profit within about a year, and **"We try harder"** stayed its slogan for decades.

cards.title: Positioning against the leader
body: **Positioning** is the place your business holds in a customer's mind compared with the alternatives.

Customers had already ranked car rental companies, and Hertz was at the top. Avis didn't try to take that spot. It claimed the second one and gave it meaning: the company that has to work harder for you.
By naming the leader, Avis borrowed a reference point everyone already understood.

image.label: A ladder in a head, with No. 2 rung lit up
image.brief: 사람 머리 실루엣 안에 사다리. 맨 위 칸에 'No. 1'(회색), 두 번째 칸에 'No. 2 · We try harder'가 밝게 빛남. 아래 칸들은 흐릿하게. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Why an honest weakness sells.
body: The ad worked because each part supported the next:
list: **Admitting a known fact** makes the rest of the ad more believable
**Naming the leader** tells customers instantly where you fit
**Being smaller** becomes a reason: you need every customer
**Specific promises**, like clean ashtrays, make "harder" concrete
cards.callout: The weakness wasn't hidden. It became the argument.

cards.title: Then Avis started talking about No. 1.
body: Later, Avis ran messages about becoming the leader. In *Positioning* (1981), Al Ries and Jack Trout argued this was a mistake.
Their point: "We try harder" only made sense from the No. 2 spot. Talking about No. 1 threw away the position customers had accepted and put Avis back into a fight it couldn't win on size.
A strong position is a place you defend, not a step you rush past.

cards.title: The promise has to be true.
body: An underdog claim invites customers to check. If the line is long and the car is dirty, "We try harder" becomes a joke. Avis backed the ads inside the business, and staff reportedly wore "We try harder" buttons.
It also needs a clear leader. In a crowded market with no obvious No. 1, saying "No. 2" tells customers nothing.
cards.softwareNote: A small tool facing a dominant product can say "we're smaller, so the founders answer your support emails." It only works while that stays true as you grow.

cards.title: Now it's a pizza place.
body: One pizzeria in your town is famous. Tourists line up for it. Yours is the second-busiest and has good reviews for fast delivery and friendly staff.
How do you position your shop?

options.feedback: Locals already think the famous place holds that title. Your claim fights their belief instead of using it.

options.text: "Skip their line. Hot pizza at your door in 30 minutes."
options.feedback: It accepts the leader's fame and turns your difference into a reason to choose you. You must hit that 30 minutes every time.

options.text: Copy their recipe and style closely
options.feedback: It may win some spillover, but it makes you the imitation. Customers then choose the original.

cards.title: If customers already know who's No. 1, use it.
body: Place yourself against what's already in their minds, and let an honest weakness make your promise believable.
**Try it today:** name the leader your customers compare you with. Write one sentence that admits how you're different, then gives the reason that helps them.
